subject: Cognitive Science
title: Bayesian Reasoning
description: A short lesson to help you apply Bayesian Reasoning.

hook.text: A medical test is 99% accurate. You test positive. What's the chance you're sick? It depends on the base rate.

buildup.text: Bayes' theorem combines prior probability with new evidence to produce an updated belief.

discovery.text: If 1 in 10,000 have the disease, most positives are false—even with a 99% accurate test.

twist.text: Humans ignore base rates naturally. We fixate on the specific evidence and skip the background math.

climax.text: Bayesian updating is the gold standard of rational belief change: adjust proportionally to evidence strength.

punchline.text: New evidence updates belief. It doesn't replace it.

details.summary: Bayesian reasoning updates beliefs by combining prior probability with new evidence using Bayes' theorem. Most people are terrible at this intuitively, consistently overweighting new evidence and ignoring base rates. A positive test result does not mean you probably have the disease.
details.whyItMatters: Bayesian reasoning is essential for medical diagnosis, legal evidence, and risk assessment. Failing at it leads to panic, misdiagnosis, and bad policy decisions.
takeaways: Prior probability must be combined with evidence strength
People systematically ignore base rates when reasoning
Natural frequency formats make Bayesian reasoning much easier

faq.question: What is base rate neglect?
faq.answer: Base rate neglect is ignoring how common something is when evaluating evidence. A 99 percent accurate test for a disease affecting 1 in 10,000 people will still produce far more false positives than true positives.

faq.question: How can you make Bayesian reasoning more intuitive?
faq.answer: Use natural frequencies instead of percentages. Instead of saying the test is 99 percent accurate, say: out of 10,000 people, 1 has the disease and tests positive. Of the 9,999 healthy people, 100 also test positive. So only 1 out of 101 positive results is a true case.
